Wikipedia - Bondi Beach (name, pronunciation, Dharawal origin)

blocks.text: I hear it mangled at least once a day, usually from a visitor asking directions. So let me settle it: Bondi is said "BON-dye". The ending rhymes with "eye", not "ee", and the stress lands on that first syllable.

The spelling is what trips people up. Overseas visitors very reasonably read that "i" on the end as "ee" - but it isn't. Think "bond", like the secret agent, followed by "eye": BON-dye. Get the ending right and you'll sound like you've been coming here for years.

The name is Aboriginal, from the Dharawal language. It's usually traced to a word for a loud thud - the sound of waves breaking over rocks - which is exactly what you hear standing on the promenade, and it's the meaning Waverley Council records for the beach it looks after. You'll also see the word linked to the nulla nulla, the fighting stick that makes the same heavy noise on impact.

Early records spell it several ways - Bundi, Bundye, Boondye - before "Bondi" settled into common use. Once you know the meaning, the name makes perfect sense: stand on the sand for a minute and it's all around you.
Easy way to lock it in: it rhymes with "Aussie hi". Bon-dye, not Bon-dee.

items.a: "BON-dye" - "bond" followed by "eye", with the stress on the first syllable. In IPA that's /ˈbɒndaɪ/. The "i" at the end sounds like "eye", not "ee".
BON-dye. "BON-dee" is the most common mispronunciation among overseas visitors, but locals say BON-dye.

items.q: What does Bondi mean, and what language is it from?
items.a: It comes from the Dharawal language. The meaning is usually given as a loud thud - the sound of waves breaking over rocks - which is the sense Waverley Council records for the beach.
